Level with them about the setting as-presented in dungeons and dragons. The protagonists (depending on the setting to an extent obviously) have decided against a normal lifestyle of choosing a trade, mastering it, and raising a family to instead roam from place to place asking after dangerous situations that people need resolved in exchange for money. And that's in the best case. In the worst case, they explore the wilderness looking for abandoned tombs and pilfer them of their (well-protected) goods.

It's a lifestyle of danger and risk, and you want to portray that in your setting. That sometimes means that the world will present rewards that are beyond your characters' current abilities to engage. If they choose to continue in their folly, it may kill their character.

If they still don't bite then you may have to compromise. Roleplaying is a cooperative story telling exercise after all. If they don't want to participate in the types of stories you want to tell then you're left with either changing the stories or changing the players.

There are some other systems that are more narrative driven and less about emergent stories (a la classical D&D). Where dice and stats decide outcomes in a situation rather than ticks on a health tracker with the only outcome being death. FATE and the gamut of Powered by the Apocalypse systems are two that immediately come to mind.

Your players and you have to have a certain amount of overlap in what you want out of the game.

You want their actions to have meaning and consequences. If the players don't, your play styles might not be compatible and you might have to kick them all out. Players are easy to replace.

The players might not want consequences, or they simply might not realize they want consequences.

Personally, I'd recommend just roleplaying the world as appropriate. If they piss off the noble, they goofed and he's done with them. Just start adding consequences. If they die and freak, they aren't right for your game and can leave. But if you start adding consequences to more minor actions they made start to understand the danger in the world and act more carefully.

You have to run a game you enjoy, bottom line. You are putting WAY more effort into this than they ever will.

The other thing I'd recommend is reading The Angry GM. He explains the importance of all this and so much more. If there are no consequences, your players are just fucking around and will not have nearly as meaningful an experience.

another angle is where the party wishes they were dead. you can torture them, figuratively speaking.

All their well laid plans go off the rails. They return to their city after an adventure to discover that it is in the middle of the third day of being pillaged after an invading army takes over. All of their collected treasure, etc is gone.

the trick here is that it looks like a well planned conventional dungeon crawl, and when they get back outside, the world has changed.

Natural disasters happen. Political disasters happen. Invasions happen. Plagues happen.

A passing comet comes by and scorches the planet (a local but semi-divine disaster), they were saved because they were underground in the dungeon. They try to leave early, and they discover the world in literal flames.

The basic big trick is being creative with what the players are doing, so that small oversights on their part becomes an opportunity for something else to come in and take advantage of them.

This is always delayed and devious. Things always have bigger consequences.

An argument starts a bar fight

a bar fight starts a riot. (party leaves town)

A riot starts a confrontation with the city guard.

This starts a local uprising (things were tense anyhow)

The uprising starts a rebellion

A rebellion starts a civil war . .

Party returns to town to find everything in chaos, Hears the story of how the rebellion started with a barfight, but no one knows who started the fight , and the stories have exaggerated everything in some fanciful way.

ooops. Now they can't get paid or whatever.

If the PC's fail to achieve their goals, the way to address that is usually not to say "game over." The game continues... and the PC's now must deal with the consequences of their failure.

Fail to stop the evil guy before he summons Orcus into the world? Welp, now there's an avatar of Orcus sitting on the capitol city, and lots of people are dying or are now undead. What are the PC's gonna do about that?

In the event of a TPK, there are a couple of options. They can either: A) roll up new characters, which come from a different part of the world, and get another crack at it. Or B) start the next campaign years or even decades after the first, in a ruined world where the PC's lost.

You have 2 options, adjust the players, or adjust the campaign.

If you chose to adjust the players, there are many, many valid consequences besides death. Nobel kicked you out? Now locals are afraid to do business with you. Can't spend that gold if the Nobel has put a death penalty over NPC's for aiding you. Give the local constables a higher level Mage. Spells like Wall of Iron or Stone are great for imprisoning PC's. Do they have lot's of shiny loot and magic items? Be a shame if a high level thief were to swipe it. Do they have Holy characters? Paladins/Clerics/Druids? If they are not following the tenets of the deity, they lose their spells. Oh , you're a mage? Gosh, it would be terrible, if the locals hated you, and would not let you rest in the Inn. Remember, magi need time to memorize spells. Also, play your intelligent monsters like intelligent monsters. Pick up Dragon Mountain Boxed set and read through that. You will learn all kinds of ideas. My players respected Kobolds after that.

An alternative would be to adjust your campaign to the play style of the players. This is the better option IMHO. Remember, the 1st rule of Gaming: Have fun. That means everyone. Don't forget that. You are working with the players to have a good time and tell a story. Many times people play RPG's to be something they are not. You can't be a Wizard in real life. That's what games are for. Sometimes, even good people like to play an Evil AntiPaladin. Let Loose. Have fun.

An Assassin's guild campaign. Again, all character types can be useful

A campaign where the players conquer the world. This can be a hoot, as players try to raise armies, take over lands, and maintain their empire.

Them being stupid makes this hard. Now the game is their story in your world so they are allowed to be stupid, and you should not punish them for doing things their way instead of your way it just makes it no fun to play THEIR adventure. That said if they are ignoring all logic and won't play in a way that lets them fail, maybe punish discourage them by altering the path to something they had planned. The evil wizard is protected by an impenetrable force wall but the noble can get them into a ball he is hosting in two days letting them go in and to face him before he sends out his army to attack the town that hired them in 2 weeks, the barbarian over does it in a sparing match with the noble's son cutting off his arm who was named on the invite and supposed to lead them there so the noble parts ways. Now they have to travel to a cave where an associate of the wizard guards the escape portal 2 weeks ride away. They go this route kill the guard face the wizard kill him finding out the army has already been sent out, they take some horses and rush back to the town finding out that the army arrived just as they killed the wizard and broke the army's organization, thus the town was able to fend them off... eventually though they lost many people and buildings and some of the fleeing army stole goods when running away. The town pays them the gold they promised but the magical items were stolen there are no healing potions left in town as they were all used and the brewer killed getting the last batch to fighters holding the line, the blacksmith leading the defense of the merchant district was killed and his smithy raided and destroyed in a fire that spread to the general goods store. The noble they offended is publicly shaming them for maiming his son that was a captain in the town guard and though he can't get them kicked out or the reward removed he ruins any good will they had with the town. They have a reduced reward their ability to immediately spend it on upgraded gear is removed, and the town is openly upset with them raising prices both now and forever as they know the town would have been safe if the barbarian could just control himself. This give penitalties both now and lasting later when they are trying to track down a set of +5 full plate armor for the paladin but the only place with any for sale is this town and remembering their actions they want double the rate that anywhere else is charging. It also sets you up for the noble sending thieves after them later on leading to a story arch where they have to return to deal with the upset noble who has been getting them robbed in the night since they were stupid and didn't have a guard duty when sleeping.

All of that is no death and even stills see them rewarded, while keeping the noble you worked on creating but twisting him from ally to enemy.

All that said another option is to run some premade campaigns then it isn't you setting the challenge but the game and if they die well not your fault, and maybe one of them will want to run one and then they can see it from your side and it will spark a change in them.

All else if you can't find a work around and they refused to work in the worlds you want to run (if both sides are not enjoying it the game ends up sucking) you may need to look for new players, sorry.

TLDR, find something there then death as a penalty or find new players (though mostly it is ideas of other ideas and a little story telling)
